title: Lessons From A Year Building With LLMs
talk_summary: A six-author keynote (O'Reilly white paper) covering strategic, operational, and tactical lessons from a year of building LLM apps. The tactical section is the actionable core: decompose evals into simple assertions, use LLM-as-judge early then fine-tuned classifiers at scale, inspect production data regularly with versioned traces, and add cheap reference-free guardrails.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of scoring an amorphous output blob, break it into named dimensions (title, price, rating; or factual consistency, relevance, density) and write simple assertions per dimension.
takeaways.evidence_quote: break it down into Dimensions such as factual inconsist y relevance and informational density and once you've done that assertion based test can go a long way

takeaways.technique: LLM-as-judge for prototyping, fine-tuned classifier for scale
takeaways.what_they_do: Use LLM judges early because they are trivial to prototype with few-shot good/bad examples, but note they need chain-of-thought (5-8s) and constant re-alignment; a fine-tuned classifier runs in ~10ms and is more precise once you have a few hundred to a few thousand labeled samples.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you have a simple classifier or reward model every request is maybe 10 milliseconds long that's two orders of magnitude lower
takeaways.numbers: LLM judge CoT 5-8s vs classifier ~10ms (2 orders of magnitude)

takeaways.technique: Reference-free evals reused as production guardrails
takeaways.what_they_do: Build evals that compare output to the source document (e.g., does the summary entail or contradict the source) rather than to a gold sample, then reuse the same check as a runtime guardrail on all new output.

takeaways.technique: Regular data inspection with versioned traces
takeaways.what_they_do: Look at production outputs regularly (a Slack channel per new agent, then daily batches), slice failures by source/keyword/topic, and tag each trace with the git commit, model version, and prompt version so it can be replayed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when you're inspecting traces it's super helpful to be able to know you know what GitHub commit or what model version or prompt version that this correspond to

takeaways.technique: Pin model versions; treat models as swappable SaaS
takeaways.what_they_do: Pin exact model versions because API behavior drifts in hard-to-quantify ways, and be willing to drop a model quickly when a competitor is clearly better.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when using llms as apis pin model version

takeaways.technique: Cheap table-stakes guardrails on all outputs
takeaways.what_they_do: Run basic automated guardrails (toxicity, PII, copyright, expected language) on every output because defects are an order of magnitude cheaper to prevent than to catch and fix.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the amount of energy to catch and fix defects is an order of magnitude larger than needed to produce it
